title: Apple Foundation Models: Swift Developer Guide
description: Build on-device AI with Apple's FoundationModels framework. Type-safe output, tool calling, and Private Cloud Compute for Swift developers.
author: Sophie Cave
content:
Apple shipped a 3-billion-parameter language model inside every device running macOS 26, iOS 27, and iPadOS 27. Not behind an API. Not in a cloud. On the chip. The FoundationModels framework gives Swift developers direct access to that model with type-safe structured output, constrained decoding, tool calling, and streaming — all running on the Neural Engine with zero network latency.

This is not a wrapper around someone else's API. This is Apple building inference into the operating system the same way they built Core ML, Vision, and NaturalLanguage. The difference is that FoundationModels is a general-purpose language model, not a task-specific classifier. You can generate text, extract entities, classify content, summarize documents, and call tools — all with compile-time type safety that no cloud API can match.

We run a production Swift server on Apple Silicon (M3 Max, 64GB) and have already integrated FoundationModels into our Vapor backend for quiz generation, summarization, and content classification. This guide covers everything we learned — from first import to production patterns — so you can ship on-device AI in your own Swift apps.

What You Get

The FoundationModels framework exposes Apple's on-device model through a clean Swift API. Here is what the framework provides:

  • On-device inference via the Neural Engine. No network calls. No API keys. No per-token billing. The model runs on the same hardware that runs your app.
  • Structured output via the @Generable macro. Define a Swift struct, annotate it, and the model's output is constrained to valid instances of that type. No JSON parsing. No validation. The compiler enforces the schema.
  • Tool calling via the @Tool macro. Define Swift functions as tools, and the model can call them during generation with type-safe arguments. Same concept as Claude's tool use, but compiled into your binary.
  • Streaming for real-time output. Partial results arrive as the model generates, so your UI can update incrementally.
  • Image input for multimodal tasks. Pass images alongside text prompts for visual understanding.
  • Private Cloud Compute for tasks that exceed the on-device model's capability. Apple routes the request to their secure cloud infrastructure with the same privacy guarantees — your data is never stored, never logged, never used for training. Free for Small Business Program members.
  • Custom adapters via LoRA fine-tuning. Train lightweight adapters on your own data and deploy them alongside the base model. The adapter files are roughly 160MB.

Requirements

Before you write any code:

  • macOS 26+ (Tahoe), iOS 27+, or iPadOS 27+
  • Xcode 26+ with the latest SDK
  • Apple Silicon — the Neural Engine is required for on-device inference. Intel Macs are not supported.
  • Apple Developer Program membership for distribution (free for on-device development)

If you are on Apple Silicon with the latest OS, you can start building right now. No entitlements needed for basic on-device inference. Private Cloud Compute and custom adapters require separate entitlements from Apple.

First Inference

The simplest possible FoundationModels code:

import FoundationModels

let session = LanguageModelSession()
let response = try await session.respond(to: "Explain retrieval-augmented generation in two sentences.")
print(response.content)  // Plain text output

That is it. No API key. No client initialization. No HTTP request. The model loads from the OS, runs inference on the Neural Engine, and returns a response. On an M3 Max, first inference takes roughly 2 seconds (model loading), subsequent calls complete in under 500ms for short prompts.

The LanguageModelSession maintains conversation history automatically. Each call to respond includes the full conversation context, so the model can reference previous turns:

let session = LanguageModelSession()
let first = try await session.respond(to: "What is MCP?")
let followup = try await session.respond(to: "How does it compare to function calling?")
// followup.content references the MCP explanation from the first turn

Structured Output with @Generable

This is where FoundationModels pulls ahead of every cloud API. The @Generable macro constrains the model's output to valid instances of a Swift type. The model cannot produce invalid JSON, missing fields, or wrong types — the decoding is constrained at generation time, not validated after.

import FoundationModels

@Generable
struct QuizQuestion {
    @Guide(description: "The question text")
    var question: String
    
    @Guide(description: "Four answer choices")
    var choices: [String]
    
    @Guide(description: "Index of the correct answer (0-3)")
    var correctIndex: Int
    
    @Guide(description: "Brief explanation of why the answer is correct")
    var explanation: String
}

let session = LanguageModelSession()
let quiz: QuizQuestion = try await session.respond(
    to: "Generate a quiz question about the Model Context Protocol.",
    generating: QuizQuestion.self
)

print(quiz.question)       // Guaranteed String
print(quiz.choices.count)  // Guaranteed [String]
print(quiz.correctIndex)   // Guaranteed Int

The @Guide macro provides descriptions that steer the model's generation for each field. Think of it as inline documentation that the model reads during inference — not comments for humans, but constraints for the AI.

You can nest @Generable types for complex output structures:

@Generable
struct LessonSummary {
    var title: String
    var keyPoints: [String]
    var difficulty: Difficulty
    var prerequisites: [String]
    var quiz: QuizQuestion  // Nested @Generable type
}

@Generable
enum Difficulty: String {
    case beginner, intermediate, advanced
}

Enums work too. The model's output is constrained to one of the defined cases. No parsing, no validation, no "the model returned 'Beginner' instead of 'beginner'" bugs. The compiler handles it.

Why This Matters

Every cloud API — Claude, GPT, Gemini — returns text that you parse into structured data. Even with JSON mode, you handle parsing errors, missing fields, type mismatches, and malformed responses. With @Generable, the type system guarantees the output shape at compile time. Your app either compiles with valid types or it does not compile at all. This eliminates an entire class of runtime errors that every cloud-API-based application has to handle.

Tool Calling

FoundationModels supports tool calling with the same type safety as structured output. Define a tool as a Swift struct with @Tool, and the model can invoke it during generation:

@Tool
struct SearchBrain {
    @Guide(description: "The search query to find relevant brain entries")
    var query: String
    
    func call() async throws -> String {
        // Your actual search implementation
        let results = await brainAPI.search(query: query, limit: 3)
        return results.map { $0.summary }.joined(separator: "\n")
    }
}

@Tool
struct GetCurrentDate {
    func call() async throws -> String {
        let formatter = DateFormatter()
        formatter.dateStyle = .full
        return formatter.string(from: Date())
    }
}

let session = LanguageModelSession(tools: [SearchBrain.self, GetCurrentDate.self])
let response = try await session.respond(
    to: "What did we ship last week?"
)
// The model calls SearchBrain with a relevant query,
// gets results, and synthesizes an answer

Tool calling on-device means tool execution stays local too. The model decides which tool to call, calls it with type-safe arguments, receives the result, and continues generation — all without a network roundtrip. For applications that need to query local databases, read files, or interact with system services, this is transformative.

Streaming

For UI applications, streaming lets you show output as it generates rather than waiting for the complete response:

let session = LanguageModelSession()

for try await partial in session.streamResponse(to: "Summarize this article.") {
    // partial.content updates incrementally
    updateUI(with: partial.content)
}

Streaming works with structured output too — you get partial @Generable instances as fields are populated. The UI can show the question text before the choices are generated, creating a progressive disclosure experience.

System Prompts and Instructions

Configure the model's behavior with system-level instructions:

let instructions = """You are a technical writing assistant for a software documentation team. 
Write in active voice. Keep sentences under 25 words. 
Use code examples for every concept."""

let session = LanguageModelSession(instructions: instructions)
let response = try await session.respond(
    to: "Explain how WebSocket connections work."
)

Instructions persist across the session. Every respond call includes them automatically. Use instructions for role definition, output style, domain constraints, and safety guardrails.

Private Cloud Compute

The on-device model is roughly 3 billion parameters. For tasks that need more capability — long documents, complex reasoning, nuanced generation — Private Cloud Compute (PCC) routes the request to Apple's secure cloud infrastructure.

Key guarantees from Apple:

  • No data retention. Your data is processed and discarded. Apple does not store prompts, responses, or any intermediate state.
  • No training. Your data is never used to train or improve Apple's models.
  • Verifiable security. PCC runs on custom Apple Silicon servers with a hardened OS. Independent auditors can verify the software running on PCC nodes.
  • Transparent routing. Your app can check whether a request was processed on-device or in the cloud.

PCC is free for developers in the Small Business Program (under $1M annual revenue). For most indie developers and small teams, this means unlimited cloud AI at zero marginal cost.

let session = LanguageModelSession()

// Check availability
let availability = session.modelAvailability
switch availability {
case .available:
    // On-device model ready
case .cloudRequired:
    // Will route to Private Cloud Compute
case .unavailable:
    // Model not available on this device
}

Vapor Integration (Server-Side Swift)

If you run a Swift server on Apple Silicon — as we do with Vapor — you can import FoundationModels directly into your server code. No API calls. No external dependencies. The model runs in your server process.

import Vapor
import FoundationModels

func routes(_ app: Application) throws {
    app.post("api", "v1", "ai", "generate") { req async throws -> Response in
        let input = try req.content.decode(GenerateRequest.self)
        
        let session = LanguageModelSession()
        let response = try await session.respond(to: input.prompt)
        
        return Response(
            status: .ok,
            body: .init(string: response.content)
        )
    }
    
    app.post("api", "v1", "ai", "quiz") { req async throws -> QuizQuestion in
        let input = try req.content.decode(QuizRequest.self)
        
        let session = LanguageModelSession()
        let quiz: QuizQuestion = try await session.respond(
            to: "Generate a quiz question about: \(input.topic)",
            generating: QuizQuestion.self
        )
        
        return quiz  // Codable, so Vapor encodes to JSON automatically
    }
}

This gives you a zero-cost AI backend. No API billing. No rate limits. No cold starts. The model is always loaded and ready. For applications that can run on a single Apple Silicon machine — which is more applications than most people think — this eliminates the entire AI infrastructure cost.

When to Use FoundationModels vs Cloud APIs

FoundationModels is not a replacement for Claude or other cloud models. It is a complement. The decision matrix:

Use CaseBest ChoiceWhy
Structured extractionFoundationModelsType-safe output, zero latency
Quiz/flashcard generationFoundationModels@Generable enforces format
Content classificationFoundationModelsEnum constraints, fast inference
Short summarizationFoundationModelsOn-device speed, no cost
Complex reasoningClaudeLarger model, deeper analysis
Long document analysisClaude200K context window vs 4K
Code generationClaudeStronger code understanding
EmbeddingsOllama/VoyageFoundationModels has no embed API
RAG retrievalHybridFM for query expansion, Claude for synthesis
Tool-heavy agentsClaudeMore sophisticated tool orchestration

The hybrid approach works. Use FoundationModels for fast, structured, on-device tasks. Use Claude for complex reasoning and long-context work. Use local embedding models for vector search. Each model handles what it does best.

Custom LoRA Adapters

Apple supports fine-tuning the on-device model with LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters. You train a lightweight adapter on your domain data and ship it alongside your app. The base model stays the same — the adapter adjusts its behavior for your specific use case.

Adapter training requires:

  • Training data in the format Apple specifies (prompt-completion pairs)
  • Apple Silicon Mac with sufficient RAM (16GB minimum, 64GB recommended for larger datasets)
  • Create ML or the command-line training tools from Apple
  • Foundation Models Adapter entitlement from Apple Developer

The resulting adapter is roughly 160MB — small enough to bundle with your app or download on first launch. Once loaded, it modifies the base model's behavior without replacing it.

Use cases for custom adapters:

  • Domain vocabulary: Medical, legal, or technical terminology that the base model handles poorly
  • Output style: Matching your brand voice, documentation format, or communication style
  • Task specialization: Improving performance on a specific task (classification, extraction, summarization) for your domain

App Intents Integration

With iOS 27, SiriKit is deprecated. App Intents is the replacement — and it integrates directly with FoundationModels. Your app's intents become tools that Siri (powered by Apple Intelligence) can invoke with natural language.

import AppIntents
import FoundationModels

struct SearchCoursesIntent: AppIntent {
    static let title: LocalizedStringResource = "Search Courses"
    static let description = "Find courses on a specific AI topic"
    
    @Parameter(title: "Topic")
    var topic: String
    
    func perform() async throws -> some IntentResult {
        let courses = CourseStore.shared.search(topic: topic)
        return .result(
            value: courses.map { $0.title }.joined(separator: ", ")
        )
    }
}

// User says: "Hey Siri, find courses about MCP servers"
// Siri invokes SearchCoursesIntent with topic: "MCP servers"

If you are building an iOS app and plan to submit to the App Store, App Intents is no longer optional. Apple is pushing hard on Siri integration, and apps without App Intents will miss out on the primary discovery mechanism in iOS 27.

Python SDK

Apple also ships a Python SDK for FoundationModels, which means you can use the on-device model from Python scripts running on Apple Silicon:

pip install apple-fm-sdk
from apple_fm import LanguageModelSession

session = LanguageModelSession()
response = session.respond("Classify this text as positive, negative, or neutral.")
print(response.content)

This is useful for data pipelines, research scripts, and tools that already run in Python. You get the same on-device inference without rewriting everything in Swift. The Python SDK wraps the same underlying framework, so performance characteristics are identical.

Performance Benchmarks

Numbers from our M3 Max (64GB) running macOS 26:

TaskApple FMOllama (qwen3:27b)Claude API
First inference (cold)~2s~3s~1.5s
Short generation (warm)~300ms~800ms~1.2s
Structured output~400ms~1.5s (JSON parse)~1.5s
Tool call roundtrip~500ms~2s~2.5s
Cost per 1K tokens$0$0$0.003-$0.075
PrivacyFull (on-device)Full (local)Cloud-based

Apple FM wins on structured output speed because the type constraint eliminates retry-parse loops. It wins on cost because there is no cost. It loses on reasoning depth because 3B parameters cannot match 100B+ cloud models. The hybrid strategy handles this — fast tasks stay on device, complex tasks go to Claude.

Xcode 27 and MCP

One more thing worth noting for developers in the MCP ecosystem. Xcode 27 ships with native MCP support and built-in Claude/Anthropic integration. Your existing MCP servers — the ones you built for Claude Code — work inside Xcode natively. The IDE connects to your MCP servers and uses them during code generation, debugging, and documentation.

This means the MCP servers you build today are not just for Claude. They are for every tool that adopts the protocol — and Apple just made Xcode one of those tools.

Getting Started Checklist

  1. Update to macOS 26 and Xcode 26 (or later)
  2. Add import FoundationModels to a Swift file and confirm it compiles
  3. Create a LanguageModelSession and run a basic respond call
  4. Define your first @Generable struct and generate structured output
  5. Add a @Tool that queries your app's data
  6. Benchmark against your current AI approach (API latency, cost, accuracy)
  7. Apply for the Small Business Program if you qualify (free PCC)
  8. Request adapter entitlements if you plan to fine-tune

Build AI-Native Apps

We build on-device AI applications and MCP integrations for Swift and Python teams. If you are integrating Apple Intelligence into your app, we can help.

What This Changes

Apple shipping a language model in the OS changes the economics of AI features. Before FoundationModels, every AI feature required an API key, a billing account, and a prayer that your cloud provider would not change pricing. Now, basic AI capabilities — classification, extraction, summarization, generation — are free infrastructure. They ship with the OS. They cost nothing to run.

This does not replace cloud AI. Claude, GPT, and Gemini handle complex reasoning, long documents, and sophisticated agent workflows that a 3B on-device model cannot match. But it shifts the floor. The baseline AI capability that every app can assume is no longer zero — it is a 3-billion-parameter model with type-safe structured output, tool calling, and streaming, running locally with zero latency and zero cost.

For Swift developers, the path is clear: start building with FoundationModels for the tasks it handles well, keep Claude for the tasks that need more power, and ship apps that are smarter than anything you could have built with either approach alone.

faqs.question: What is Apple FoundationModels?
faqs.answer: Apple FoundationModels is a Swift framework introduced in macOS 26 and iOS 27 that gives developers direct access to Apple's on-device language model. It runs a roughly 3-billion-parameter model on the Neural Engine with no API calls, no internet connection, and no per-token cost. It supports text generation, structured output via the @Generable macro, tool calling, streaming, and image input.

faqs.question: Is Apple FoundationModels free to use?
faqs.answer: Yes. On-device inference with FoundationModels is completely free — it runs on the device hardware with no API billing. Private Cloud Compute, which handles heavier tasks in Apple's secure cloud, is also free for developers enrolled in the Small Business Program (under $1M annual revenue). There are no per-token charges for either on-device or cloud inference.

faqs.question: What devices support Apple FoundationModels?
faqs.answer: FoundationModels requires Apple Silicon. It runs on any Mac with an M1 chip or later (macOS 26+), any iPhone with A17 Pro or later (iOS 27+), and any iPad with M1 or later (iPadOS 27+). Intel Macs are not supported because the framework relies on the Neural Engine for inference.

faqs.question: How does @Generable work in Apple FoundationModels?
faqs.answer: @Generable is a Swift macro that constrains the model's output to valid instances of a specific type. You annotate a Swift struct or enum, and the model generates output that matches that type's shape exactly. Fields are populated with correct types, enums are constrained to defined cases, and nested types are handled automatically. This eliminates JSON parsing errors and validation code.

faqs.question: Can I use Apple FoundationModels in a Vapor server?
faqs.answer: Yes. If your Vapor server runs on Apple Silicon (M-series Mac), you can import FoundationModels directly into your server code. The model runs in your server process with no external API calls. This gives you a zero-cost AI backend with no rate limits, no API keys, and no cold starts.

faqs.question: How does Apple FoundationModels compare to Claude?
faqs.answer: FoundationModels runs a 3B-parameter model on-device with zero cost and zero latency, but with a 4,096-token context window and limited reasoning depth. Claude offers 200K+ token context, stronger reasoning, and more sophisticated agent capabilities but requires API calls and per-token billing. The best approach is hybrid — use FoundationModels for fast structured tasks and Claude for complex reasoning.

faqs.question: What is Private Cloud Compute?
faqs.answer: Private Cloud Compute (PCC) is Apple's secure cloud AI infrastructure. When a task exceeds the on-device model's capability, the request is routed to Apple's cloud servers running on custom Apple Silicon. Apple guarantees no data retention, no training on your data, and verifiable security. PCC is free for Small Business Program members.

faqs.question: Can I fine-tune Apple's on-device model?
faqs.answer: Yes, through LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters. You train a lightweight adapter on your domain data using Create ML or Apple's command-line tools. The adapter is roughly 160MB and modifies the base model's behavior without replacing it. You need the Foundation Models Adapter entitlement from Apple and an Apple Silicon Mac for training.

faqs.question: Does Apple FoundationModels support embeddings?
faqs.answer: No. FoundationModels does not include an embedding API. For vector embeddings, use a local model like mxbai-embed-large via Ollama or a cloud service like Voyage AI. FoundationModels handles text generation, structured output, and tool calling — embeddings remain a separate concern.

faqs.question: What happened to SiriKit in iOS 27?
faqs.answer: SiriKit is deprecated in iOS 27. Apple replaced it with App Intents, which integrates directly with Apple Intelligence and FoundationModels. Apps should migrate to App Intents for Siri integration, Spotlight suggestions, and Shortcuts. App Intents uses the same type-safe Swift patterns as FoundationModels, and your intents become tools that Siri can invoke with natural language.
